ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory FINTRAC-compliant customer due diligence and enhanced due diligence for a medium-risk enhanced luxury resale platform: (i) positive-match screening of all UBOs, directors, authorized signatories and high-value consignment counterparties against UN Security Council consolidated lists, Criminal Code s 83.05 listed entities, Special Economic Measures Act schedules, Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act (Magnitsky) listings, and FINTRAC-published lists; (ii) politically exposed persons (PEP) screening using FINTRAC definitions of foreign PEP, domestic PEP and head of an international organization, with risk-based enhanced continuous monitoring; (iii) contractual OFAC SDN screening and Stripe/Escrow.com prohibited-business interdiction screening because payment rails settle in USD, notwithstanding that OFAC listings are not directly domesticated in Canadian law; (iv) luxury resale red-flag monitoring for trade-based money laundering, over/under-valuation of consigned goods, identity spoofing, rapid flipping from high-risk source jurisdictions, and counterfeit/trademark-infringing inventory; (v) 90-day refresh of KYC data and transaction monitoring alerts for unusual wire, escrow-release or payment-flow patterns.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: BC Corporate Online (Corporate and Land Registry, Government of British Columbia) - corporateonline.gov.bc.ca
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Statutory requirement that the corporate name use Roman-alphabet characters; English and French are accepted. Non-Latin scripts (for example Chinese characters in the founder's brand) must be transliterated into a romanized legal name, and the romanized name must be distinctive so as not to be confusing in sound or appearance with any existing BC or federal name. The legal name may be supplemented by a bilingual or secondary name where the underlying intellectual property is non-Latin, but the registered BC legal name must remain storable and searchable in Roman form.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: BC name reservations are non-renewable and valid for 56 days; upon expiry the applicant must file a new name request and pay the applicable statutory fee. If the name is refused for confusing similarity or a prohibited/sensitive token, the applicant may (i) submit a written reconsideration request to the Registrar of Companies at the BC Corporate Registry within 30 days of refusal, attaching factual evidence of distinctiveness or a letter of consent from the holder of the conflicting name; (ii) where refusal is grounded on a regulated token, obtain the prior written approval or consent of the relevant regulator (for example the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions for bank/insurance terms); (iii) if the Registrar affirms the refusal, apply for judicial review in the Supreme Court of British Columbia under the Judicial Review Procedure Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c 241, or, as a practical alternative, re-file with a new distinctive element (for example a coined brand or UBI-style descriptor) and preserve marketing identity through a registered BC trademark filing.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: A virtual office or mail-forwarding address is not permissible as the BC registered office. BCBCA s 20 requires a physical street address in British Columbia where the statutory records and the transparency register are accessible during business hours. Registered-agent physical addresses, such as the offices of the incorporating law firm, are compliant, provided that the registered office is not a post-office box. A virtual office may be used only as a separate mailing or logistics address; it cannot satisfy the registered-office obligation.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low (estimated less than 5% annual probability for a compliant online-only luxury resale company). The BC Registrar and FINTRAC conduct announced administrative compliance reviews and desk-based examinations rather than routine unannounced physical inspections. Unannounced site visits may exceptionally be triggered by a search warrant in connection with police or proceeds-of-crime investigations, counterfeit luxury goods enforcement, or a FINTRAC compliance examination escalation.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (central bank and monetary authority); foreign exchange surveillance and financial-crime compliance oversight are jointly administered by the Department of Finance Canada, the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI), and the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC). Canada does not maintain a dedicated exchange-control authority and has no general system of foreign-exchange licensing.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Canada maintains fully convertible current-account and capital-account regimes under IMF Article VIII obligations. There are no exchange controls, no central bank approval requirements for capital injections, and no restrictions on the conversion or repatriation of profits, dividends, interest, or liquidation proceeds. The Canadian dollar (CAD) is a freely floating currency. The only compliance hurdles are indirect: cross-border payments above CAD 10,000 trigger FINTRAC electronic funds transfer reporting; dividend payments to non-resident shareholders are subject to Canadian Part XIII withholding tax unless reduced by an applicable tax treaty; and transactions with listed sanctioned jurisdictions or persons must be screened under the Special Economic Measures Act and United Nations Act.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: There are no statutory surrender requirements, mandatory conversion ratios, or designated timelines for the repatriation of export proceeds in Canada. Exporters may lawfully maintain foreign-currency bank accounts and retain earnings offshore. However, the exporter must report certain cross-border electronic transfers of CAD 10,000 or more to FINTRAC under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act, and must keep accurate books and records to substantiate income inclusion for Canadian tax purposes under the accrual method. For vintage luxury resale, all sale proceeds from online transactions must be traceable through the intermediary platform's settlement reports to satisfy anti-money-laundering (AML) and tax record-keeping obligations.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility rating: Medium-to-High for auxiliary treasury operations, with important legal constraints. Canadian-chartered banks remain the primary liquidity and clearing partners because they provide settlement certainty under the Canadian Payments Act and access to the Lynx system. Offshore Electronic Money Institutions (EMIs) may support operational foreign-currency accounts and cross-border payment execution, but they generally cannot offer a Canadian-dollar clearing account routed through Lynx unless they partner with a Canadian bank or hold a FINTRAC money services business (MSB) registration for remittance services. Any foreign EMI operating as a payment service provider to Canadian residents must assess whether it crosses the threshold for FINTRAC MSB registration; Canadian corporate clients using foreign EMIs remain fully responsible for record-keeping, source-of-funds documentation, and tax compliance. For a vintage luxury resale business holding consumer-facing settlement funds, segregated fiduciary accounts held at a Tier-1 Canadian bank are the legally safer routing than unregistered offshore EMI accounts.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Canadian banks typically require at least one director, the ultimate beneficial owner, or the authorized account signatory to complete an in-person identity verification at a Canadian branch. Remote verification is increasingly permitted under FINTRAC's client identification rules when the bank uses dual-process electronic identity proofing, biometric facial comparison, and a live video interview, but most Tier-1 commercial banks still impose a physical presence or a notarized/certified true-copy package for non-resident directors. For a British Columbia corporation, the incorporator or a director should ideally attend a Canadian branch in Vancouver or Toronto; remote-only onboarding is generally available only for a trusted existing banking relationship or where the financial institution has a dedicated high-net-worth digital onboarding platform that includes a live interview with an AML compliance officer. The mandate can be satisfied by a combination of: (1) a certified copy of the certificate of incorporation, (2) the federal and/or British Columbia registration record, (3) corporate register excerpts confirming directors and shareholders, (4) source-of-wealth evidence, and (5) a video interview held during Canadian business hours.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Luxury resale e-commerce model flagged as high-risk because of secondhand goods, cross-border counterparties, and multiple payment channels.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide audited transaction history from the online marketplace (Stripe, Escrow/Pay), a detailed seller verification policy, authentication certificates for luxury items, third-party appraisal reports, chain-of-custody documentation for consignment inventory, and a written AML risk self-assessment evidencing that each consignor is identified, that provenance is verified, and that no cash-intensive activity is present.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident director or shareholder, particularly originating from a jurisdiction perceived as high-risk or non-cooperative for tax purposes.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide a certified copy of a valid passport, proof of residential address, professional reference letters from a regulated financial institution, a tax-residency certificate, a corporate organigram disclosing the full beneficial-ownership chain, and a comfort letter from a Canadian legal counsel explaining the commercial rationale and source of funds.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Large inbound capital injection from an offshore jurisdiction inconsistent with the stated equity capital and start-up profile.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide executed share subscription agreements, bank statements of the ultimate transferring account, board resolutions approving the capital contribution, completion certificates for funds verification (SWIFT MT103 confirmation), proof of the transferor's source of wealth (tax returns, audited financial statements, or sale-and-purchase agreements), and a notarized declaration of funds.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Cross-border trade disbursements to vendors in jurisdictions with known sanctions or money-laundering vulnerabilities.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide a counterparty sanctions-screening report, know-your-customer (KYC) and know-your-buyer (KYB) documentation for each vendor, supplier invoices, authentication reports for the vintage goods purchased, transport and logistics bills of lading, and an internal compliance gateway confirming that all counterparties are absent from the Consolidated Canadian Autonomous Sanctions List, the UN sanctions list, and OFAC SDN list.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Escrow payment and consumer refund flows creating perceived layering, commingling, or unverified third-party payments.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide a detailed flow-of-funds diagram separating buyer payments, seller disbursements, escrow holdbacks, refunds, fees, and platform settlement reports; execute a written escrow agreement; maintain a segregated client-transaction ledger; and provide monthly reconciliation reports as well as a written confirmation from the payment processor that the merchant account is verified and owned solely by the Canadian entity.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: The compliant routing for inbound equity or subordinated-loan capital is a SWIFT MT103 international wire transfer from the foreign investor's bank to the Canadian corporation's operational or escrow account at a Tier-1 Canadian bank. The beneficiary account should be identified with the Canadian bank's institution number, transit/branch number, and account number; the beneficiary legal name must exactly match the corporate name in the articles. The wire must be accompanied by an inward remittance advice specifying the purpose as 'equity contribution / share subscription' or 'loan advances' in plain business language. Although Canada does not issue exchange-control purpose codes, the bank's automated compliance system will capture the remittance narrative, so the narrative should contain a reference to the corporate name and the share subscription agreement. For an injection exceeding CAD 10,000, the receiving bank is required to file a FINTRAC EFT report; the corporate treasury must therefore be prepared to provide source-of-wealth documentation and the board resolution. All capital should be routed to the same account from funding accounts owned by the exact shareholders recorded in the corporate register; third-party payments should be avoided outright or accompanied by a clear collateral assignment and declaration of trust.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Outbound trade payments from the Canadian entity will be executed by SWIFT MT103 for direct vendor payments, or via a commercial documentary letter of credit (LC) issued by the Canadian bank for high-value consignment purchases requiring shipment security. Domestic Canadian-dollar payments may be cleared through the Lynx real-time gross settlement system for large amounts or the Automated Clearing Settlement System (ACSS) for standard payments; partner-financed legacy rails are not recommended. For cross-border USD payments, the Canadian bank may route through its United States correspondent or use the bank's US-dollar clearing account. Acceptable clearing instruments include: (a) SWIFT MT103 for pre-paid vendor invoices and authenticated luxury-goods purchases; (b) SWIFT MT700 / MT707 for irrevocable documentary credits with vendor-favorable performance and transport documents; and (c) escrow-initiated disbursements via SWIFT MT103 supported by the escrow agent's release instructions. The corporate treasury must maintain a documentary archive for each disbursement: invoice, contract, transport insurance, export/import customs declaration, authentication certificate, and FINTRAC EFT report record where applicable.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable FX forward contracts with a Canadian Schedule I bank for committed USD/CAD purchases or sales
Non-deliverable currency forwards (NDFs) where CAD is the reference currency and settlement is netted in USD when counterparty restrictions apply
Cross-currency interest rate swaps (CIRS) for aligning debt-service currencies and minimizing refinancing risk
FX swaps and rollover forwards used for short-term working-capital liquidity matching
Plain-vanilla FX options (call or put) purchased to hedge uncertain future trade flows

Commodity or luxury-good price hedges are irrelevant; currency hedges must be specifically documented as treasury risk-management transactions and should not create speculative trading positions under bank internal policies

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No size/revenue-based mandatory audit threshold for a private BC corporation. Auditor appointment is mandatory only for distributing/public or reporting-issuer corporations; private BC companies may dispense with an auditor by unanimous shareholder consent (BCBCA) or by unanimous shareholder resolution under CBCA.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: IFRS (CPA Canada Handbook Part I) or Canadian ASPE (Part II); a private e-commerce luxury resale corporation will normally adopt ASPE unless shareholders require IFRS.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: For each share transfer or issuance, update the central securities register and register of members before the transfer is deemed complete. Confirm/refresh the register of individuals with significant control (ISC) at least annually at the directors' annual review; this annual confirmation supports the corporate annual return certification that registers are complete. The ISC/transparency register is maintained in the corporate records and is not filed with the regulator, except that federal CBCA annual return requires confirmation of compliance.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Individuals with Significant Control (ISC/UBO)
